thread.title: Rift develops between community farm founder, current board
thread.title_full: Rift develops between community farm founder, current board

author: ohtadmin
title: Rift develops between community farm founder, current board
text:
More than produce has sprung up this past week at the Jamestown Community Farm as the former manager and its current board of directors have become at odds with each other.
Bob Sutton, who founded the farm on Eldred Avenue in 2000 and served as its manager the first 24 years, locked the gate to the farm July 20 due to “two serious and unresolved personnel issues,” according to a message he posted that night on a Jamestown community Facebook page.
The lock was cut off the next morning and the farm is operating as usual.
Sutton’s post said he did this “because the Jamestown Community Farm Inc. is legally responsible to the landowner for the safety of the farm workers and the protection of his property.”
Since the landowner, Peter Ceppi, lives in Florida and Sutton has known him for more than 30 years, he said locking the gate was his attempt to try to protect Ceppi’s interest in case anything legally actionable occurred at the farm, Sutton said.
“In my mind, it was a way of saying Peter’s not responsible for this,” he said. “I just felt responsible for the whole thing.”
Sutton declined to elaborate on what the “personnel issues” are or why they’re “unresolved.” He said his attempts to discuss these issues with the board have come to no avail.
Mark Liberati, who is a member of the farm’s board of directors, said Sutton is “raising issues that are not issues.”
“Our position is the board has done everything in accordance with the law and bylaws and that’s it,” he said.
Liberati said Sutton’s issue stems from the fact he disagrees with the choice of Greg Godsey as the new farm manager, but the board’s procedure to select Godsey followed its rules.
Sutton’s wife, Lynda, who helped co-found the farm, stepped down from the board after the vote to hire the new manager, whom she opposed.
Sutton, who is not on the board, acknowledged that the couple preferred another applicant, believing her educational background and experience were far greater and more relevant to what the local farm does and needs.
Sutton also said he is concerned the farm is moving away from its core ideals and that could lead to longer-term problems.
“When members don’t take care of business, their organization gradually fails,” he said. “My concern is that continuing on the present path jeopardizes the farm’s funding, its volunteer work-partners and its 501(c)3 nonprofit status.”
The dispute led a small group of people to rally outside the farm this past Saturday morning. The event was organized by Denise Rounds in support of the Suttons, whom she has known for years and whose children volunteered at the farm.
“The rally was to support the Suttons and create more awareness that there are issues,” Rounds said.
“Thanks to all of you and I apologize,” Sutton’s Facebook post ended. “All my wife and I ever wanted to do was grow fresh, local vegetables and deliver them to people.”
Liberati said the couple’s actions the past week are hurting the very thing they say they care about.
“If Bob and Lynda’s goal is to make sure that this farm is protected in perpetuity from development, their actions in challenging the board’s decision with regard to hiring have sabotaged what should be their ultimate goal,” Liberati said.
The issue is a civil matter, and no charges have been filed, according to Capt. Angela Deneault of the Jamestown Police Department. She was made aware of the situation when a board member came to the station July 21 after the lock was cut with a copy of the closure note Sutton placed on the gate. No other action or complaint has been filed since then.

Sutton’s wife, Lynda, who helped co-found the farm, stepped down from the board after the vote to hire the new manager, whom she opposed. Sutton, who is not on the board, acknowledged that the couple preferred another applicant, believing her educational background and experience were far greater and more relevant to what the local farm does and needs.
